title: Blog about things you don't understand yet
excerpt: Every post I publish represents at least two things I’ve learned: the thing that prompted me to write the post, and the thing I learned in the course of writing it. If I don’t learn anything new while I’m writing, it’s not interesting enough to publish.
content_html:
Every post I publish represents at least two things I’ve learned: the thing that prompted me to write the post, and the thing I learned in the course of writing it. If I don’t learn anything new while I’m writing, it’s not interesting enough to publish.

Typically I learn way more than two things. For instance, in my o3 geoguessr post, I started out with the idea that most AI prompts probably don’t work, and I ended up learning that newer OpenAI models have lost o3’s ability to geolocate. That’s interesting! In my most recent post on C2PA, I started out with the idea that C2PA requires near-universal adoption, but I learned a ton of things about PKI, managing private keys on local devices, how C2PA actually works, and so on. In my post on the Luddites, I started out with the idea that the Luddite movement was fundamentally decentralized, but ended up fascinated by Luddite culture (which was far more elitist, misogynist, and violent than the pop-Luddism books describe). I could do this for every single post on the blog.

Taking a position

I think the core reason this works is that every single one of my blog posts argues a point. I never publish a post that just gives some scattered thoughts on a topic, or a post that only says “yes, I agree with this other article”. If I write a draft that nobody sensible could disagree with, I scrap the draft. Making sure that everything I write is at least minimally controversial is a forcing function: it forces me to think about what the most interesting part of my position is, and it forces me to do enough research to defend it against the obvious criticisms.

This is contrary to a lot of advice I read about blogging, which encourages the aspiring blogger to treat their posts as a form of unstructured self-expression. If unstructured self-expression is what you want to do, that’s cool. The point of having a blog is that you get to write what you want. However, this advice isn’t as helpful as it sounds.

Before I was in tech, I was a philosophy grad student. But before that, I was a poet. One thing you learn when you try to write poetry is that it is way easier to write to a restrictive structure than it is to simply “write what you feel”. This should be obvious when you actually think about it. The task of a poet is to repeatedly choose the next word. Writing to a structure (typically rhyme or meter) narrows that choice to a small set of words, instead of the entire English language. It’s the same with blogging. Forcing yourself to write about specific, potentially-controversial points makes consistently writing easier, not harder.

Writing, thinking, and research

Writing is the best way to think clearly about a topic. It’s easy to believe you understand something when you’re just turning it over in your head. When you have to condense that down into words, you find out exactly how much you do or don’t understand. I am constantly having moments where I type something, stop myself, and think “wait, that can’t actually be right”, or “is that really true?”

By the time I write my way to the end of the post, I’m usually thinking so much more clearly about the topic that my conclusion paragraph is way better than my introduction. In fact, I’ve picked up the habit of going back and immediately rewriting the first paragraph as part of my first-draft process, because I know I’m going to end up doing it anyway.

I also change my mind a lot while I write. Here are a bunch of examples of posts where I began writing them with the opposite opinion to the one that eventually made it into the post. I think this is a good sign, and I hope I never stop doing it. You should be researching and thinking about every post you write, and that means you should frequently learn new things that change your mind.

Because of all this, I deliberately choose to write blog posts about things I don’t yet quite understand but would like to, like LLM steering, Stripe’s Tempo blockchain, C2PA and watermarking, space cooling, interaction models, LLM inference internals, and so on. This is great for me, because I learn a lot. Is it great for my readers?

Is blogging to learn irresponsible?

I sometimes worry that I should only be writing about areas I already know very well, like tech company dynamics or working in large codebases, rather than presenting myself as an authority on fields I’m actually still learning. Should I let historians of the Luddites write about Luddism, Web3 engineers write about blockchains, and so on? I think this is acceptable for three reasons.

First, it’s sometimes easier for a beginner to write an introduction to a field than for an expert. Experts routinely overestimate the knowledge of the general public, and have often internalized the reasons why their field is important so deeply that they struggle to express them. I think my explainer posts are valuable because I always spend the first chunk of the post talking about what the original problem is before I get into the technical solution.

Second, sometimes the public consensus on a topic is just plain wrong, to the point where even a little bit of research is enough to demonstrate why. Many of my posts I’m proudest of have been along these lines: arguing that the “500ml per prompt” water usage figure for LLMs was ludicrous, or that the popular Apple “Illusion of Thinking” paper was tracking persistence, not reasoning, that GPUs live longer than three years and the AI companies have large profit margins on inference, and so on.

Third, I try to make it clear on my blog who I am and what my credentials actually are. Even if it’s not explicitly described in the post, I have my real name and resume available on my /about page, so I don’t think a careful reader could be easily fooled into thinking I’m an expert on 19th-century England or space physics or LLM economics or anything like that.

Feedback

Even if nobody reads what you write, writing is still a good discipline for getting your thoughts in order. But another big reason why writing is a great learning tool is that you can get feedback.

I think it’s obvious why this is useful, but I do want to make two points about feedback. First, if you do make your posts public, you need to have a pretty thick skin. People on the internet often fall over themselves to come up with the most cutting criticism or the harshest dunk. This goes double if you take my previous advice and try to write posts that make a clear, controversial point about a subject you’re learning. If you’re the kind of person whose whole day is ruined when a stranger is cruel to them, you might want to keep your blogging private or only share it among friends.

Second, even if your blogging is private, you can get feedback from LLMs. Like humans, LLMs will often give junk feedback. In my experience, OpenAI models will always tell me to moderate my claims or add caveats and hedges until I’m not saying anything at all. Sometimes their criticism will be straight-up wrong. But — particularly about technical topics — LLMs are great at pointing out areas you’ve genuinely misunderstood, and they’re far kinder than the average Lobsters or Hacker News commenter.

Conclusion

I’m pleased and grateful that people enjoy reading my posts, but even when nobody did, I still got a lot of value out of blogging. I write as a method of thinking more clearly, as an excuse to do research on topics I want to learn about, and as a way of getting feedback.

If you’d like to try it yourself, I suggest watching for these two things. First, you should be changing your mind a lot as you write. If not, you probably aren’t doing enough research. Second, your first draft’s conclusion should be much tighter and more expressive than its introduction. If not, you probably haven’t learned anything from the writing process, which means the draft can be scrapped.

I strongly recommend this practice to anyone with an interest in writing. You will see the benefits even if you don’t publish any of your writing on the internet, particularly now that you can get good technical feedback by pasting your post into an LLM1.

  1. For what it’s worth, I’ve fiddled with careful “review prompts” and it’s basically as good to just write “review, please:” and paste your article.

Saying the obvious thing

Stating the obvious is surprisingly useful. Most of your knowledge lives below the threshold of conscious awareness, so it’s possible for a piece of writing to remind you of what you already know. It’s common to know you don’t like something without being quite sure why, and reading an obvious statement (such as “accuracy matters, even when you agree with the broad strokes”) can help clarify why you find certain things distasteful.

blocks.html_en: Because of all this, I deliberately choose to write blog posts about things I don’t yet quite understand but would like to, like LLM steering, Stripe’s Tempo blockchain, C2PA and watermarking, space cooling, interaction models, LLM inference internals, and so on. This is great for me, because I learn a lot. Is it great for my readers?

sentences.en: Because of all this, I deliberately choose to write blog posts about things I don’t yet quite understand but would like to, like LLM steering, Stripe’s Tempo blockchain, C2PA and watermarking, space cooling, interaction models, LLM inference internals, and so on.
sentences.zh: 正因为如此，我特意选择撰写关于我还不太了解但想要了解的内容的博客文章，例如 LLM 指导、Stripe 的 Tempo 区块链、C2PA 和水印、空间冷却、交互模型、LLM 推理内部结构等等。

sentences.zh: 这对我来说很棒，因为我学到了很多东西。

sentences.en: Is it great for my readers?
sentences.zh: 这对我的读者来说很棒吗？

blocks.html_en: Is blogging to learn irresponsible?

sentences.en: Is blogging to learn irresponsible?
sentences.zh: 写博客来学习是不负责任的吗？

blocks.html_en: I sometimes worry that I should only be writing about areas I already know very well, like tech company dynamics or working in large codebases, rather than presenting myself as an authority on fields I’m actually still learning. Should I let historians of the Luddites write about Luddism, Web3 engineers write about blockchains, and so on? I think this is acceptable for three reasons.

sentences.en: I sometimes worry that I should only be writing about areas I already know very well, like tech company dynamics or working in large codebases, rather than presenting myself as an authority on fields I’m actually still learning.
sentences.zh: 有时我担心我应该只写我已经非常了解的领域，比如科技公司动态或在大型代码库中工作，而不是在我实际上仍在学习的领域表现出自己的权威。

sentences.en: Should I let historians of the Luddites write about Luddism, Web3 engineers write about blockchains, and so on?
sentences.zh: 我是否应该让卢德派历史学家写关于卢德主义的文章，让 Web3 工程师写关于区块链的文章，等等？

sentences.en: I think this is acceptable for three reasons.
sentences.zh: 我认为这是可以接受的，原因有三个。

blocks.html_en: First, it’s sometimes easier for a beginner to write an introduction to a field than for an expert. Experts routinely overestimate the knowledge of the general public, and have often internalized the reasons why their field is important so deeply that they struggle to express them. I think my explainer posts are valuable because I always spend the first chunk of the post talking about what the original problem is before I get into the technical solution.

sentences.en: First, it’s sometimes easier for a beginner to write an introduction to a field than for an expert.
sentences.zh: 首先，初学者有时比专家更容易编写某个领域的介绍。

sentences.en: Experts routinely overestimate the knowledge of the general public, and have often internalized the reasons why their field is important so deeply that they struggle to express them.

sentences.zh: 我认为我的解释性帖子很有价值，因为在进入技术解决方案之前，我总是用帖子的第一部分来讨论原始问题是什么。

blocks.html_en: Second, sometimes the public consensus on a topic is just plain wrong, to the point where even a little bit of research is enough to demonstrate why. Many of my posts I’m proudest of have been along these lines: arguing that the “500ml per prompt” water usage figure for LLMs was ludicrous, or that the popular Apple “Illusion of Thinking” paper was tracking persistence, not reasoning, that GPUs live longer than three years and the AI companies have large profit margins on inference, and so on.

blocks.html_en: Third, I try to make it clear on my blog who I am and what my credentials actually are. Even if it’s not explicitly described in the post, I have my real name and resume available on my /about page, so I don’t think a careful reader could be easily fooled into thinking I’m an expert on 19th-century England or space physics or LLM economics or anything like that.

blocks.html_en: Feedback

sentences.en: Feedback
sentences.zh: 反馈

blocks.html_en: Even if nobody reads what you write, writing is still a good discipline for getting your thoughts in order. But another big reason why writing is a great learning tool is that you can get feedback.

sentences.en: Even if nobody reads what you write, writing is still a good discipline for getting your thoughts in order.

sentences.en: But another big reason why writing is a great learning tool is that you can get feedback.
sentences.zh: 但写作是一种很好的学习工具的另一个重要原因是你可以获得反馈。

blocks.html_en: I think it’s obvious why this is useful, but I do want to make two points about feedback. First, if you do make your posts public, you need to have a pretty thick skin. People on the internet often fall over themselves to come up with the most cutting criticism or the harshest dunk. This goes double if you take my previous advice and try to write posts that make a clear, controversial point about a subject you’re learning. If you’re the kind of person whose whole day is ruined when a stranger is cruel to them, you might want to keep your blogging private or only share it among friends.

blocks.html_en: Second, even if your blogging is private, you can get feedback from LLMs. Like humans, LLMs will often give junk feedback. In my experience, OpenAI models will always tell me to moderate my claims or add caveats and hedges until I’m not saying anything at all. Sometimes their criticism will be straight-up wrong. But — particularly about technical topics — LLMs are great at pointing out areas you’ve genuinely misunderstood, and they’re far kinder than the average Lobsters or Hacker News commenter.

blocks.html_en: Conclusion

sentences.en: Conclusion
sentences.zh: 结论

blocks.html_en: I’m pleased and grateful that people enjoy reading my posts, but even when nobody did, I still got a lot of value out of blogging. I write as a method of thinking more clearly, as an excuse to do research on topics I want to learn about, and as a way of getting feedback.

sentences.en: I write as a method of thinking more clearly, as an excuse to do research on topics I want to learn about, and as a way of getting feedback.
sentences.zh: 我写作是一种更清晰思考的方法，是对我想了解的主题进行研究的借口，也是获得反馈的一种方式。

blocks.html_en: If you’d like to try it yourself, I suggest watching for these two things. First, you should be changing your mind a lot as you write. If not, you probably aren’t doing enough research. Second, your first draft’s conclusion should be much tighter and more expressive than its introduction. If not, you probably haven’t learned anything from the writing process, which means the draft can be scrapped.

content_html_zh:
我发布的每一篇文章都至少代表了我学到的两件事：促使我写这篇文章的东西，以及我在写这篇文章的过程中学到的东西。 如果我在写作时没有学到任何新东西，那么它就不够有趣，无法发表。

通常我学到的东西不止两件事。 例如，在我的 o3 geoguessr 帖子中，我一开始认为大多数 AI 提示可能不起作用，最终我了解到较新的 OpenAI 模型已经失去了 o3 的地理定位能力。 那很有意思！ 在我最近关于 C2PA 的文章中，我一开始就认为 C2PA 需要近乎普遍采用，但我学到了很多有关 PKI、管理本地设备上的私钥、C2PA 实际工作原理等方面的知识。 在我关于勒德分子的文章中，我一开始认为勒德运动从根本上来说是去中心化的，但最终却对勒德文化着迷（它比流行的勒德主义书籍所描述的更加精英主义、厌恶女性主义和暴力）。 我可以对博客上的每一篇文章执行此操作。

采取立场

我认为这种方法有效的核心原因是我的每一篇博客文章都论证了一个观点。 我从来不会发表一篇只给出一些关于某个主题的零散想法的帖子，或者一篇只说“是的，我同意另一篇文章”的帖子。 如果我写的草稿没有任何明智的人会反对，我就会废弃该草稿。 确保我写的所有内容至少具有最小的争议性是一种强制功能：它迫使我思考我的立场中最有趣的部分是什么，它迫使我做足够的研究来捍卫它免受明显的批评。

这与我读到的许多关于博客的建议相反，这些建议鼓励有抱负的博客作者将他们的帖子视为一种非结构化的自我表达形式。 如果你想做的是非结构化的自我表达，那就很酷。 拥有博客的意义在于您可以写自己想要的内容。 然而，这个建议并不像听起来那么有帮助。

在进入科技行业之前，我是一名哲学研究生。 但在此之前，我是一名诗人。 当你尝试写诗时你会学到的一件事是，按照限制性结构写作比简单地“写你的感受”要容易得多。 当你真正思考时，这一点应该是显而易见的。 诗人的任务是反复选择下一个词。 按照结构（通常是韵律或格律）进行写作会将选择范围缩小到一小部分单词，而不是整个英语。 博客也是如此。 强迫自己写下具体的、可能有争议的观点会让持续写作变得更容易，而不是更困难。

写作、思考和研究

写作是清晰思考主题的最佳方式。 当你在脑子里翻阅某件事时，很容易相信你已经理解了它。 当你必须将其浓缩为文字时，你就会发现自己到底理解了多少或不理解多少。 我经常会遇到这样的情况：我输入一些东西，然后停下来思考“等等，这实际上不可能是正确的”，或者“这是真的吗？”

当我写到文章的结尾时，我通常会更清楚地思考这个主题，所以我的结论段落比我的介绍要好得多。 事实上，我已经养成了回去并立即重写第一段的习惯，作为我初稿过程的一部分，因为我知道无论如何我最终都会这样做。

我在写作的过程中也改变了很多想法。 这里有一堆帖子的例子，我开始写这些帖子时所持的观点与最终发表在帖子中的观点相反。 我认为这是一个好兆头，我希望我永远不会停止这样做。 你应该研究和思考你写的每一篇文章，这意味着你应该经常学习改变你想法的新事物。

正因为如此，我特意选择撰写关于我还不太了解但想要了解的内容的博客文章，例如 LLM 指导、Stripe 的 Tempo 区块链、C2PA 和水印、空间冷却、交互模型、LLM 推理内部结构等等。 这对我来说很棒，因为我学到了很多东西。 这对我的读者来说很棒吗？

写博客来学习是不负责任的吗？

有时我担心我应该只写我已经非常了解的领域，比如科技公司动态或在大型代码库中工作，而不是在我实际上仍在学习的领域表现出自己的权威。 我是否应该让卢德派历史学家写关于卢德主义的文章，让 Web3 工程师写关于区块链的文章，等等？ 我认为这是可以接受的，原因有三个。

首先，初学者有时比专家更容易编写某个领域的介绍。 专家们经常高估公众的知识，并且经常将他们的领域如此重要的原因内化到他们难以表达的程度。 我认为我的解释性帖子很有价值，因为在进入技术解决方案之前，我总是用帖子的第一部分来讨论原始问题是什么。

其次，有时公众对某个主题的共识完全是错误的，甚至一点点研究就足以证明原因。 我最引以为傲的许多帖子都是这样的：认为法学硕士“每次提示 500 毫升”的用水量数字是荒谬的，或者流行的苹果“思维幻觉”论文跟踪的是持久性，而不是推理，GPU 的寿命超过三年，人工智能公司在推理上有很大的利润空间，等等。

第三，我尝试在我的博客上明确我是谁以及我的凭据实际上是什么。 即使帖子中没有明确描述，我的真实姓名和简历也可以在我的 /about 页面上找到，所以我认为细心的读者不会轻易被愚弄，认为我是 19 世纪英国、空间物理学、法学硕士经济学或类似领域的专家。

反馈

即使没有人读你写的东西，写作仍然是一种很好的纪律，可以让你的想法井井有条。 但写作是一种很好的学习工具的另一个重要原因是你可以获得反馈。

我认为这为什么有用是显而易见的，但我确实想就反馈提出两点。 首先，如果你确实要公开你的帖子，你的脸皮就得足够厚。 互联网上的人们常常不遗余力地提出最尖锐的批评或最严厉的扣篮。 如果你采纳我之前的建议，尝试写一些帖子，对你正在学习的主题提出清晰的、有争议的观点，那么情况会加倍。 如果您是那种因为陌生人对自己残忍而一整天都被毁掉的人，您可能希望将您的博客保密或只在朋友之间分享。

其次，即使您的博客是私人的，您也可以从法学硕士那里获得反馈。 和人类一样，法学硕士经常会给出垃圾反馈。 根据我的经验，OpenAI 模型总是会告诉我要缓和我的主张或添加警告和限制，直到我什么也不说。 有时他们的批评是完全错误的。 但是，尤其是在技术主题方面，法学硕士非常擅长指出你真正误解的领域，而且他们比一般的龙虾或黑客新闻评论者要友善得多。

结论

我很高兴也很感激人们喜欢阅读我的帖子，但即使没有人这样做，我仍然从博客中获得了很多价值。 我写作是一种更清晰思考的方法，是对我想了解的主题进行研究的借口，也是获得反馈的一种方式。

如果您想自己尝试一下，我建议您注意这两件事。 首先，你在写作时应该经常改变你的想法。 如果没有，您可能没有进行足够的研究。 其次，初稿的结论应该比引言更紧凑、更富有表现力。 如果没有，你可能没有从写作过程中学到任何东西，这意味着草稿可以被废弃。

我强烈向任何对写作感兴趣的人推荐这种做法。 即使您不在互联网上发表任何文章，您也会看到好处，特别是现在您可以通过将您的帖子粘贴到 LLM1 中来获得良好的技术反馈。
